newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco companies ask for judgment in Broin case.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco companies ask for judgment in Broin case.

text.p: Tobacco company lawyers Wednesday asked a Florida judge to toss out key elements of a landmark secondhand-smoke lawsuit, arguing that lawyers for U.S. flight attendants had failed to prove that tobacco companies committed fraud.

The case, known as Broin vs. Philip Morris et al., was scheduled for trial on Monday. It was filed on behalf of some 60,000 flight attendants who claim they contracted a variety of maladies, including lung cancer, from breathing cigarette smoke on U.S.-based passenger jets.

In arguing a tobacco industry motion for summary judgment on allegations that the companies committed fraud and conspiracy, attorney Hugh Whiting said the flight attendants had failed to prove that any statement made by a specific tobacco executive had any impact on decisions made by any specific flight attendant.

"There is no evidence in this case, no factual evidence in this case ... that anybody made a misstatement to anyone," said Whiting, who represents RJ Reynolds Tobacco Co, a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp.

Whiting also argued that any lobbying efforts made by tobacco companies were protected by constitutional free-speech rights and therefore could not be used as a basis for a fraud claim. He said tobacco companies had no duty to make safety disclosures to people who had not bought their products.
"Here, no plaintiff has any relationship with any defendant," Whiting said. "They never bought a product; they never used a product."

Plaintiffs' attorney Susan Rosenblatt said the motion for summary judgment had no merit, arguing that members of the class action had continually been misled by cigarette producers over a period of decades to believe that secondhand smoke presented no health risk.

She cited tobacco company documents and advertisements issued during a broad U.S. public debate about the risks of smoking in public places, saying the tobacco companies knew that if smoking became socially unacceptable "it would impact on their sales."
"They wanted to reassure non-smokers, including our flight attendants, there was no risk," she said. "You sure have a duty when you tell people that secondhand smoke is safe to not lie."

Dade County Judge Robert Kaye did not indicate when he would decide the issue. A ruling in favor of the tobacco companies would eliminate key elements of the case -- that the industry had engaged in a broad-based conspiracy over many years to mislead the American public into thinking that tobacco smoke was safe.
United States Tobacco Co, a unit of UST Co Inc and the largest U.S. seller of smokeless tobacco, asked Wednesday to be excused from the case.
In a brief argument for a summary judgment, a company lawyer said at no time in six years of litigation on the Broin case had anyone linked any of its products to any plaintiff.
The company stopped manufacturing cigarettes in 1985 and at its peak held only two-tenths of one percent of the U.S. market. Kaye did not immediately rule on the request.
